damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 — Snape introduces Occlumency lessons in the Potions classroom after Arthur Weasley's attack
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Snape delivers the Occlumency mandate privately at Grimmauld Place, in a tense scene with Sirius present, full of psychological gamesmanship: Snape goads Sirius about his uselessness, baits Harry, and demonstrates calculated cruelty mixed with professional authority. The scene is rich with the Snape-Sirius dynamic and Snape's layered motivation.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film collapses the Grimmauld Place scene entirely. Snape simply appears in the Potions classroom and delivers exposition about Occlumency with minimal dramatic context. The entire Snape-Sirius confrontation — including Snape's deliberate psychological attack on Sirius's sense of worth, Sirius drawing his wand, and Harry being caught between them — is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Grimmauld Place scene is the primary textual establishment of the Snape-Sirius dynamic in this book. Snape's precise cruelty toward Sirius ('frustrated by the fact that you can do nothing useful') and Sirius's wounded pride are causally important: Dumbledore later acknowledges Snape's goading contributed to Sirius's recklessness. Cutting this removes a key link in the chain leading to Sirius's death, and strips Snape of his most revealing moment of calculated psychological aggression in the corpus.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 — Snape's Occlumency lesson delivery: 'You're just like your father: lazy, arrogant... weak'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Snape during Occlumency lessons is harsh and contemptuous but frames his attacks in terms of Harry's failures of discipline and control. His insults are pointed at Harry's emotional incontinence ('Fools who wear their hearts proudly on their sleeves... weak people'). He is also shown as genuinely, if coldly, attempting to instruct — noting improvement, explaining theory at length, and revealing discomfort when Harry breaks into his memories.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Snape calls Harry 'lazy, arrogant... weak' in a blunt, personally hostile register that reads as pure contempt. The line 'Your father was a swine' — delivered in response to Harry saying 'My father was a great man' — has no equivalent in the book corpus. In the book, Snape's pedagogical cruelty is more procedural and clinical; the film renders him as simply vindictive and personally hateful.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Snape uses insults instrumentally, embedded in actual teaching. The film's blunt 'Your father was a swine' collapses his complexity into straightforward villainy, removing the ambiguity that makes the Pensieve revelation and Harry's eventual sympathy ('I just never thought I'd feel sorry for Snape') emotionally coherent. It also pre-empts the Pensieve's impact by stating Snape's hatred of James explicitly rather than letting it emerge through memory.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 — Snape terminates Occlumency lessons after the Pensieve intrusion: 'Your lessons are at an end. Get out.'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Snape is white with rage, physically shakes Harry, throws him bodily, and screams at him — a rare complete loss of composure that signals how profoundly violated he feels. Crucially, Harry reflects at length on feeling genuine sympathy for Snape and understanding his humiliation. Snape's termination of lessons is an emotional rupture with real consequences Dumbledore later calls a critical mistake.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Snape grabs Harry by the jacket and says 'Enough. Your lessons are at an end. Get out.' The termination is abrupt and cold rather than a breakdown. The physical and emotional violence of the book scene — the thrown jar, the shaking, the screaming — is absent, as is Harry's subsequent internal reflection on feeling sorry for Snape.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's breakdown scene is essential to Snape's characterization as someone whose wounds around James Potter run genuinely, dangerously deep — something Dumbledore explicitly names as his own mistake in trusting Snape to overcome it. The film's cold dismissal presents Snape as simply cutting off a student, losing the revelation that beneath his control is a traumatized person. This also undermines Dumbledore's later confession that he was wrong about Snape's ability to heal.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 — Pensieve sequence: James's bullying of Snape rendered without Snape's retaliatory hex or Lily's intervention dynamic
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Pensieve scene shows Snape retaliating against James with a Sectumsempra-like curse that slashes James's face before being hung upside down again. Snape calls Lily a 'filthy little Mudblood' when she tries to help him — a moment of devastating self-destruction that explains why their friendship ended. The scene presents Snape as both victim and agent: humiliated but also capable of cruelty toward the one person defending him.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Pensieve shows James casting Expelliarmus and humiliating Snape, then James saying 'Right. Who wants to see me take off Snivelly's trousers?' The scene cuts away before Snape's retaliation and before Lily's intervention. There is no 'Mudblood' moment, no depiction of Snape destroying his own rescue, and no Lily present as a meaningful figure in Snape's memory.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book Pensieve scene does double work: it complicates James (Harry's idol) and it complicates Snape (the villain) simultaneously. Snape's 'Mudblood' outburst against Lily is the hinge on which his entire tragic arc turns — it is the moment that ended his friendship with the woman he loved and set him on the path to Voldemort. Without it, the Pensieve is merely a bullying scene rather than a window into Snape's formative wound. The film loses the material that makes Snape's eventual redemption arc (across the saga) legible.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 — Snape's response to Harry's 'Padfoot' warning in Umbridge's office
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Snape's response to 'He's got Padfoot at the place where it's hidden' is described as inscrutable — Harry cannot tell if Snape understood. Snape plays it off coldly in front of Umbridge. Dumbledore later confirms Snape immediately understood, contacted the Order, gave Umbridge fake Veritaserum, and attempted to search the Forest. His apparent indifference is a cover; his competence and loyalty are retrospectively validated.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Snape responds to 'Padfoot' with 'I'm afraid you've used up all my stores interrogating students... Unless you wish to poison him... I cannot help you.' He then leaves. When Umbridge asks 'What is Padfoot?', the film Snape does not respond and simply departs. There is no subsequent confirmation in the film corpus that Snape acted on the warning or alerted the Order.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses this scene as partial vindication of Snape's loyalty — Dumbledore explicitly confirms Snape decoded Harry's message and acted immediately. The film presents Snape's exit as ambiguous at best and indifferent at worst, with no payoff confirming his action. This damages his function as a covert operative and removes a crucial data point in the book's argument that Snape, despite his hatred of Harry, is fundamentally on the right side.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 — Snape's Occlumency lesson framing: absence of Snape storing memories in the Pensieve before each lesson
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book repeatedly and explicitly shows Snape removing his own memories and storing them in the Pensieve before each Occlumency lesson — a detail Harry observes, wonders about, and which directly enables the Pensieve intrusion. It establishes Snape's vulnerability, his deliberate self-protection, and Harry's growing curiosity about what he is hiding.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film shows no equivalent ritual. The Pensieve is not shown as a recurring feature of the Occlumency setup in the film corpus. The Pensieve intrusion in the film occurs but lacks the buildup of Harry repeatedly watching Snape perform this ritual and wondering about its contents.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The repeated Pensieve ritual in the book makes Harry's eventual intrusion feel earned and psychologically motivated — he has been watching Snape guard something for weeks. Without this setup, the intrusion reads as more random. It also strips away a layer of Snape's characterization: a man so protective of his inner life that he physically removes memories before allowing Harry near his mind.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 — Snape's Occlumency teaching reduced to two brief sessions with minimal instructional content
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book devotes extensive material to multiple Occlumency sessions over months, showing Snape's teaching methodology (theory, repeated attempts, specific feedback), Harry's incremental and then regressing progress, and Snape's conflicted reactions when Harry accidentally breaks into his memories. Snape also explicitly explains Legilimency theory, Voldemort's use of it, and the stakes.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film compresses Occlumency to what appears to be one or two brief scenes. The extended pedagogy, multiple sessions, Harry's worsening connection to Voldemort correlated with the lessons, and Snape's layered reactions across weeks are absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Occlumency arc is central to both Harry's and Snape's characterization in Order of the Phoenix. For Harry, it is a months-long struggle that paradoxically worsens his Voldemort connection. For Snape, it is a prolonged test of his ability to suppress personal hatred in service of duty — one he ultimately fails. The film's compression removes the arc's weight, making Snape's eventual termination of lessons feel arbitrary rather than the culmination of a sustained, fraught relationship.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Snape's cameo at Grimmauld Place ('How touchingly paternal, Black. Perhaps Potter will grow up to be a felon, just like his godfather')
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes that Snape visits Grimmauld Place regularly but Harry never comes face to face with him during these visits — the glimpses are fleeting and Harry is deeply curious about Snape's Order role. The Grimmauld Place Snape-Sirius confrontation occurs in a dedicated private scene with Harry present.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film gives Snape a brief appearance during the group gathering at Grimmauld Place, where he delivers the line 'How touchingly paternal, Black. Perhaps Potter will grow up to be a felon, just like his godfather.' This is a compressed substitute for the much richer private confrontation scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While the line conveys Snape's contempt, it reduces the Snape-Sirius dynamic to a one-liner in a crowd scene. The book's private confrontation — with its extended psychological warfare, wand-drawing, and Harry caught between them — is the scene that establishes the full weight of their mutual hatred and its consequences. The film substitution is too thin to carry that relational damage.

main_damage_causes: Compression and near-elimination of the multi-month Occlumency arc removes the central sustained Snape-Harry dynamic of the book, losing both Snape's complex pedagogy and his ultimate failure of duty over personal hatred
Excision of the Grimmauld Place confrontation scene strips the Snape-Sirius relationship of its psychological depth and severs the causal chain linking Snape's goading to Sirius's fatal recklessness

Truncation of the Pensieve scene — omitting Snape's 'Mudblood' outburst against Lily — removes the single most important piece of Snape's backstory available in this book, collapsing his tragic arc into simple victimhood without the self-destructive agency that makes him a complex figure
